html:
This bar covers Australia and New Zealand as British settler colonies and then independent countries: Australia from the first British colony in 1788, New Zealand from British annexation in 1840.

Both lands were already home to peoples with long histories: the Aboriginal Australians for at least 50,000 years, and the Māori, who settled Aotearoa around 1250 to 1300. James Cook charted New Zealand in 1769 and Australia's east coast in 1770 and claimed it for Britain.

Australia began as a prison. The First Fleet landed convicts at Sydney Cove in 1788, and transportation continued until 1868. Free settlers, sheep and wool followed, and the gold rush of the 1850s brought a flood of migrants. The colonies pioneered the secret ballot. In 1901 six colonies joined as the Commonwealth of Australia, which at once adopted the White Australia policy, not fully ended until 1973.

New Zealand became British under the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, signed with Māori chiefs, though the English and Māori texts differed on what was given up. Land disputes led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s. In 1893 it became the first self-governing country to give women the vote.

Both sent troops to the world wars; the Gallipoli landing of 1915 became a founding story for both. Since the mid-20th century they have turned toward Asia and the Pacific, ended racial migration rules, and begun to address Indigenous claims, through the Waitangi Tribunal in New Zealand and native title in Australia after the Mabo case.
sum: This bar covers Australia and New Zealand as British settler colonies and then independent countries: Australia from the first British colony in 1788, New Zealand from British annexation in 1840.
